bio.medium: Sotiris Iliadis is a Thessaloniki-based Product Designer / Design Engineer with 13 years of craft. He began in graphic and brand design - community identity, packaging, and marketing assets for companies across Greece - and built a deep eye for typography, hierarchy, and visual restraint. After the Google UX Design Certificate he moved into UX/UI and, now, AI-native product design: he designs in Figma and ships in code (React, Tailwind, Astro), with AI tools (Claude, Cursor) native to the process. His work carries a responsible-AI and accessibility spine - WCAG 2.2 AA and EU AI Act transparency built into the design, not bolted on. Recent proof he built and shipped himself: the Article 50 UI Pattern Kit (open-source, MIT) - accessible React components for EU AI Act Article 50 transparency - and a live 'accountable AI' demo where a model discloses itself, streams its reasoning, shows a real confidence meter, and routes low-confidence decisions to a human, all WCAG 2.2 AA. He designs the hard part of AI products: making generative, non-deterministic experiences feel clear, trustworthy, and inclusive.

whereHeard: Directly on your careers board, while researching AI-native companies I'd genuinely want to design for.

answers.text: I've worked remote-first for years as an independent designer in Thessaloniki, with clients across timezones. What works for me is writing things down - async only holds up if decisions live in a document, not in someone's memory. So I over-communicate context (the why behind a design, not just the what), keep a visible trail, and ship in small increments so feedback comes early instead of at one big reveal. I hand off annotated Figma and written specs an engineer in another timezone can build from without waiting on me. The honest challenge is momentum and isolation - remote removes the ambient signal of a room. I handle it by setting tight personal loops and treating my AI tooling (Claude, Cursor) as an always-on collaborator between human syncs. Working across Greek and English also taught me to write plainly and confirm understanding rather than assume it.

Three things, and it's the combination that's rare. First, I came up through 13 years of visual and brand craft before moving into UX - so I bring a level of typographic and compositional restraint most product designers never built. Second, I design and ship in code (React, Tailwind, Astro), so I don't hand off static screens; I take an idea to a working, accessible interface myself. Third, I use AI (Claude, Cursor) as a native part of my process. The proof isn't a claim - it's public: I designed and shipped the Article 50 UI Pattern Kit, an open-source (MIT) React component library for EU AI Act transparency, plus a live demo of the accountable human-in-the-loop AI loop. Most designers have one or two of these; the overlap - deep visual craft, code fluency, an AI-native workflow, and shipped open-source proof - is where I'm different.

I'm extremely good at taking something complex or messy and making it feel calm, legible, and obvious - the reductive work of deciding what to remove, not what to add, from 13 years of visual craft. What I could teach a team: accessibility as craft, not compliance (WCAG-level rigor and EU AI Act transparency built into the design itself - I turned this into an open-source component kit, so it's a method I can hand over, not just a principle), and a practical AI-native workflow - how I use Claude and Cursor to prototype and ship real interfaces faster without losing craft.

I ship in the open. My clearest piece of public proof is the Article 50 UI Pattern Kit - an open-source (MIT) React component library I designed and built for EU AI Act Article 50 transparency: an AI-disclosure badge, a content label, an emotion-recognition notice, and a human-in-the-loop review gate, every component WCAG 2.1 AA with a passing axe audit. It's on GitHub (github.com/sotosili/article50-kit) and running live with a working demo of the accountable-AI loop (article50-kit.pages.dev). I build entirely on the open-source stack (Astro, Tailwind, React, shadcn/ui), and this is the direction I'm taking my design-engineering work - solving a real, unglamorous compliance problem in reusable, accessible code that anyone can adopt.

I'm a product designer and design engineer who ships in code - 13+ years in design, now building interfaces in React/Tailwind with Claude and Cursor as native tools, on a responsible-AI and accessibility spine (WCAG AA, EU AI Act). I design the hard part of AI UX: making generative, non-deterministic products feel clear and trustworthy. Recent proof I shipped myself: the open-source Article 50 UI Pattern Kit and a live demo of the accountable human-in-the-loop AI loop (article50-kit.pages.dev), plus a bilingual PWA at 94 Lighthouse with zero accessibility violations. (TAILOR ME per company - name the specific product/problem I want to work on.)

The problem I most want to design is the human-in-the-loop moment - when an AI proposes a change and a person reviews and approves it in one keystroke, with no friction and no anxiety. I cared about it enough to build a working prototype of exactly that: a review gate where a low-confidence AI decision is handed to a person to approve, override, or reject (article50-kit.pages.dev/demo). Keeping the human in control as AI does more, without adding weight, is the interaction I think about most. (TAILOR ME per company to a concrete first project.)

Stripe. They treat documentation as a product and design the developer's understanding, not just the UI - progressive disclosure, runnable examples, and a visual language calm enough that a dense API feels approachable. Linear is the other one: relentless craft and restraint, where nothing on screen is unnecessary. (TAILOR the second half per company - what could THEY specifically borrow.)
I work independently, so I'm available to start immediately or on short notice.
An AI-native product designer with 13 years of craft who designs and ships in code - I make AI products feel clear, trustworthy, and accessible.
